labels.synonym_in_intended_sense: interchangeable with the input in its intended code meaning
labels.near_synonym: close in the intended meaning, interchangeable in some code contexts
labels.alias_same_concept: another name of the same concept (product, protocol, pattern)
labels.abbreviation_correct: correct abbreviation/expansion for the intended meaning
labels.spelling_or_form_variant: spelling, hyphenation, or inflection variant of the input
labels.related_only: related concept, not the same meaning
labels.wrong_sense: valid only for a different sense of the input

method: Each record is one related term a coding agent was shown for one of its search terms. The intended meaning of `input` is its sense in `prompt` (the task the agent was searching for; prompts may be Korean, terms are English). Label `candidate` against that meaning using only the record: `source` dictionary candidates carry a relation `kind` and a sense `gloss`; `source` morphology candidates are the input with one word replaced by an inflected form found in the repository vocabulary (`kind` inflection); `source` identifier_form candidates are the input phrase written as one identifier that exists in the repository, in camelCase (search parser -> searchParser) or snake_case (test file -> test_file, found inside identifiers such as is_test_file); when the input is two terms joined by ' + ' (for example sync + external alertmanager -> syncExternalAlertmanager), judge the candidate against the two terms read together as one phrase in the task's sense. Labels are repository-independent; one label per record. Do not read any file other than the assignment.
output: one JSON object per input record, in input order: {"review_id", "case_id", "candidate", "label", "rationale"}; rationale is one short English sentence
